Let's produce.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>**Top Business Etiquette Norms for Japan** *(A quick‑reference guide for meetings, travel, and virtual engagements)* | # | Topic | Key Do’s | Common Pitfall | |---|-------|----------|--------------| | 1 | **Greeting & Bowing** | • Use a firm but respectful bow (30–45°).
• Offer a small handshake only after the bow if that’s how the person wants it. |  "Rushing through a greeting shows disrespect." | | 2 | **Business Card (Meishi) Etiquette** | • Present the card with both hands, cardinal side up.
• Receive cards with both hands and a brief, polite glance.
• Keep the card on a small holder or a leather "meishi" on the table while speaking. |  Cricket/casual handling or keeping it in a pocket. | | 3 | **Hierarchy & Deference** | • Always greet the senior-most person first.
• Keep your tone modest; avoid overt self‑promotion. |  “Up‑front boasting or speaking too loudly.” | | 4 | **Punctuality** | • Arrive 5–10 minutes early (not late).
• If delay is unavoidable, call or email immediately with an apology. |  Late arrival = “non‑respectful” or “unprofessional.” | | 5 | **Dress Code** | • Dark, conservative suits for men; tailored suits or formal dresses for women.
• Shoes should be black, clean, and non‑sporty. |  Too bright colors or a casual style (“smart‑casual” is rarely acceptable in main offices). | | 6 | **Communication Style** | • “Tatemae” (public façade) vs. “Honne” (true feelings).
• Speak politely with keigo (honorific language).
• Use indirect phrasing: “Perhaps…?” instead of blunt “no.” |  Direct “no” or confrontational tone. | | 7 | **Gift‑Giving** | • Give small, high‑quality gifts (e.g., local specialty, fine stationery).
• Present the gift with both hands and a respectful bow.
• Avoid alcohol for business clients unless invited. |  Large alcoholic bottles or souvenirs that look cheap. | | 8 | **Dining Etiquette** | • Wait for the senior to begin eating.
• “Itadakimasu” before eating; “gochisousama deshita” after.
• Use chopsticks only properly; don’t point or pass food with them. |  Stalling a table or using chopsticks to “hand‑shake.” | | 9 | **Meetings & Minutes** | • Nominate a note‑taker; meeting minutes may be shared after the fact.
• Outline agenda; stay on topic.
• Subtle hand gestures precede compliments. |  Wasted time or off‑track discussions. | |10 | **Email & Phone** | • Use proper opening/closing: “Hajimemashite,” “Yoroshiku onegaishimasu.”
• Keep emails short, to‑the‑point, and sent before 12 pm.
• Call after 10 am; late‑night calls are unacceptable. |  Long, informal, “Slack‑like” tone. | |11 | **After‑Works Socializing (nomikai)** | • Accept an invitation; showing genuine interest is valued.
• When a toast: “Kanpai” with “Kami” (first cup).
• Keep conversation polite, avoid controversial or overly personal topics. |  Declining too frequently or refusing a drink abruptly. | |12 | **Respect for Time & Consensus** | • Group decisions dominate; avoid making sweeping statements alone.
• Leave the floor to the group; allows silent “no” to be expressed. |  Trying to “force” a decision on a team. | --- ### How to Use This Cheat‑Sheet 1. **Preparation:** Make a short checklist for your trip (business cards stock, dress kits, call‑card, etc). 2. **First Meeting:** * Wear a dark suit with a subdued tie. * Greet the senior pound‑first; exchange meishi. * Listen attentively; let the senior speak first. 3. **Throughout the Visit:** * Remember that politeness + humility = trust. * When dining, observe the seating order—senior will usually sit near the head of table. * During group talks, keep your body language open but reserved. 4. **Virtual Settings:** * Video calls: dress professionally on top; keep environment tidy. * Record minutes and distribute promptly by email (follow the same greeting/closing conventions). --- ### Quick “Do / Don’t” Summary | Do | Don’t | |----|-------| | Greet politely (bow, meishi), use keigo. | Use a casual handshake for every introduction. | | Arrive early, bring a small but thoughtful gift. | Show up late or carry work materials casually in your pocket. | | Dress conservatively (dark suits, modest accessories). | Wear bright colors or sneakers. | | Speak politely, indirectly, and ruminate on consensus. | Be confrontational or deliver a blunt “no.” | | Listen first; hesitation is accepted as “honorous." | Dominate conversation or rush decisions alone. | | Accept a nomikai invitation; enjoy the toast with respect. | Decline all social invitations or refuse the first drink abruptly. | --- **Bottom line:** Demonstrate respect, humility, and patience. These are the foundations of Japanese business culture. A small gesture—like correctly handling a business card—will resonate far longer than any sales pitch. Preparing a mental “ecz”scoped around the 12 norms above is your best bet to start and maintain successful relationships in Japan. Good luck!
